i. Natural Regions of India

Paleomagnetism is the branch that studies the magnetic properties preserved in the rocks, sediments or other such things during their formation. This branch of science is helpful in the study of ancient geological phenomena.
According to continental drift theory, the Indian mainland is a part of Gondwanaland.
Gondwanaland includes present day Peninsular India, Australia, Africa, Arabian Peninsula, South America and regions of Antarctica.

In the mid Mesozoic era (Jurassic Period, 144-208 Million Years Ago), Gondwanaland split into a number of pieces through convection currents. The Indian plate started drifting towards north after splitting from Gondwanaland. Consequently, the Indian plate, moving towards north, collided with a bigger plate, called the Eurasian plate.

Due to this collision, the sedimentary rocks of the Tethys Sea, between the two plates (i.e., Indian and Eurasian), folded and developed into the Himalayas and mountain ranges of West Asia. The whole mountain range of the Himalayas represents a youthful topography. It has high peaks, deep valleys (gorges), and fast - flowing rivers. In the Terai region of the Himalayas,
artesian wells
are also found.
Due to upliftment of
Tethys Sea

in the Himalayas and the subsidence of the northern flank of the peninsular plateau, resulted in the formation of a large basin. With the passage of time, this basin was gradually filled with sedimentary deposits of rivers flowing from Northern mountains and Peninsular Plateau. In this way, a vast land area of alluvial deposits was developed as the ‘Northern Plain’ of India.
Geologically, Peninsular Plateau is the ancient part of Earth’s surface.

Peninsular Plateau is the most stable region of India. Peninsular Plateau comprises of hills and broad valleys which are made up of igneous and metamorphic rocks. Meghalaya plateau is an extension of Peninsular plateau. It was separated from Indian Peninsula through
Malda Gap
due to faulting. The Western Coast of India was formed due to faulting and subsidence of the western flank of the plateau.

The Indian mainland shows a large variation in the physical structure. Therefore India is divided into four natural regions. These are - 1. Northern Mountains 2. Northern Plains 3. Peninsular Plateau and 4. Coastal Plains & Islands.
Based on the variations in its geological structure and formations, India can be divided into 3 primary and 6 sub-physical geomorphic regions

Great Himalaya is the oldest range, formed in the Eocene and Oligocene epochs (37-24 million years ago). Afterwards, the middle Himalaya was formed in the Miocene epoch (24- 5 Million years ago) and the Shivalik, the earliest one, was formed in the Pliocene epoch (5-2 million years ago).

Mountain Range situated in the northern part of the Himalayas is called the Greater or Higher Himalayas or Himadri. It is the most continuous range which has the highest peaks with an average height of 6000 meters.
Northern and North - Eastern Mountains

is the highest peak in the world located in the Great Himalayas. It is situated on the boundary of Nepal and Tibet.

a, the third highest peak in the world, lies in the Himalayas. It lies between the Teesta River in the east and the Tamur River in the west. Kanchenjunga lies on the border of eastern Nepal and the Sikkim state of India.

Peak is located in north - central Nepal.

The Himalayas contain a number of Glaciers, therefore Himalayan Rivers are perennial. Ranges situated in the south of the Great Himalaya are called Lesser Himalaya/ Middle Himalaya. Its height lies between 3700 meters to 4500 meters and the average width is 50 km. Pir Panjal is the longest range in the Middle Himalayas.

The outermost range of the Himalayas is called Shiwaliks. Its width is between 10 to 50 km and height between about 900m to 1100m. These ranges are formed by - unconsolidated sediments brought by rivers from main Himalayan ranges.
The longitudinal valleys lying in between the Lesser Himalaya and the Shiwaliks is known as Duns.
Some famous Duns are - Dehradun, Kotlidun and Patlidun.

It is an alluvial fan structure made of riverine deposits. The width of the Bhabar plain is greater in the west than in the east.

runs: The Peninsular Plateau is a tableland composed of old crystalline igneous and metamorphic rocks. Delhi Ridge in the northwest (extension of Aravallis), the Rajmahal Hills in the east,
Gir Range

Shillong

This Plateau was formed due to the breaking and drifting of the Gondwana land. Broad and shallow valleys and rounded hills are its special features.
It has two broad divisions, namely, the
Central Highlands
and the
Deccan Plateau

The part of Peninsular Plateau lying to the north of the Narmada river covering a major area of the Malwa Plateau is known as the Central Highlands. The Vindhyan Range is bounded by the Central Highlands in the South and Aravallis on the north west. The Aravalli range is the oldest mountain range in India, running across Rajasthan from northeast to southwest direction, extending approximately 800km. The northern end of the range continues as isolated hills and rocky ridges into Haryana, ending near Delhi. It is formed in the
Pre Cambrian era
. Its highest peak is
Guru-Shikhar (1722m)
located in

A valley is a low area of land between hills and mountains, typically with a river or stream flowing through it. India is blessed with many valleys, famous for their scenic views and historical importance. Valleys in India are found both in Northern and Southern parts, however valleys are dominantly found in the Northern mountainous part of the country.

A Pass is a gap, or break, in high, rugged terrain such as a mountain ridge. A Pass is formed when a glacier or a stream erodes, or wears away, the land between the areas of higher terrain. Passes often provide the easiest routes for people to travel across steep mountain ranges.

A Pass is a connectivity route through the basin of a mountain or mountain ranges. In India a lot of passes are found in the Himalayan region and the Western Ghats. These passes often become an essential medium for connectivity via roadways and railways.

runs: The altitude at a particular place above which some snow remains on the ground throughout the year is called a snowline. A glacier is a slowly moving mass or river of ice formed by the accumulation and compaction of snow on mountains or near the poles.

Different areas of the Himalayas have different snowlines depending upon the differences in latitude, relief, precipitation, slope and local topography. However, the average snowline is found at a height of

Fedchenko
, situated in the Pamir Region, whereas

is the second largest glacier. Even according to the various sources available on the internet Fedchenko is the largest glacier outside the polar region and Siachen is the second largest. Hence, according to this order Sasaini is way below in the table.

The Indian peninsula was formed around 3600 million years ago. Before the Carboniferous period it was a part of Gondwana's land.
In the Carboniferous period, coal was formed in the Damodar, Son, Mahanadi and Godavari basins whereas in Cretaceous period bulk of volcanic eruptions led to the formation of Deccan Traps.
The
Deccan Plateau
is a part of Indian shield. It is made up of basaltic lava. The Deccan trap was started to form approx.
66.25 million years ago
. The Peninsular Plateau consists of both broad and shallow valleys and round topped hills.
The peninsular plateau is basically divided into two parts- The
Central Highlands
and the
Deccan Plateau

. The part of the peninsular plateau lying to the north of the Narmada river, covering a major area of the Malwa Plateau is known as the Central Highlands.The Central Highlands are broad towards the west and start narrowing down towards the east. The eastward extension of the Central Highlands is sometimes locally known as
Bundelkhand
and
Baghelkhand
Plateau of India
The River Damodar Drains the
Chotanagpur Plateau

which is a part of central highlands. The Chotanagpur Plateau mainly extends from Ranchi in Jharkhand to Hazaribagh, Santhal Pargana division, Palamu, Dhanbad, East and West Singhbhum districts, Purulia, Bankura, West Medinipur district of West Bengal and Mayurbhanj and Sundargarh districts of Odisha.
The Chotanagpur Plateau comprises various other plateaus of different heights. In the central western part of the Chotanagpur Plateau
pats
is found, which has a maximum height of 1100 meters. All around this Plateau steps are found and the sharp break in slopes are marked by steep scarps.
The central highlands, consist of rivers like
Chambal
Sind
Betwa
and
Ken
which flow from south-west to northeast thus being a proving factor of the slope of the region.

The Malwa Plateau (length - 530 km, breadth - 390 km) covers approx 150000 km² area of Peninsular India. Its borders are determined by Aravalli in the North, Vindhya range in the south and Bundelkhand Plateau in the east.
The Deccan Plateau is a triangular landform, situated south of the River Narmada. The Satpura ranges flank its broad base in the north are
Satpura Range
while
Mahadeo
Kaimur
and
Maikal ranges

form its eastern extension. The Deccan Traps, where black soil or Regur is found which was formed as a result of weathering of lava (basalt) obtained by volcanic eruptions. Aravalli range is found in the Western and North Western parts of the Peninsular Plateau. The Aravalli Range is an eroded stub of ancient mountains and is the oldest range of fold mountains in India.
A part of the Peninsular Plateau is also found in the northeastern part of our country. Locally they are called the
Meghalaya Plateau
Karbi-Anglong Plateau
and
North Cachar Hills
. This northeastern part of the Peninsular Plateau was separated from the mainland by Malda Gap due to faulting. There are three important hill complexes in the Meghalaya Plateau, named
Garo
Khasi
and
Jaintia
Hills respectively. The Dandakaranya region of
Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Telangana, Maharashtra
and
Andhra Pradesh
spreads across an area of 89078 km².
(a) Indian Coastline
India is surrounded by water on three sides. The length of the Indian Coastline is

km. (According to data from the 1970s). As per MoPSW circular dated 29 April, 2025, the revised coastline length is 11098.81 km. The Indian coastline extends towards the Indian Ocean, dividing it into two sea: the Arabian Sea on the west and the Bay of Bengal on its east.
India has a coastline that touches
States and Union Territories.
Haveli & Daman
and Diu
Nicobar Islands
Total
The length of the coastline touching the mainland of the country is
km (Now- 7870.51 km.) long. whereas the coastline away from the mainland is
(Now- 3228.3 km.) long.
The state of
Gujarat
has the longest coastline whereas that of
Goa
is the shortest. The coastline or the seashore, is the area where land meets the sea or the ocean or a line that forms the boundary between the land and ocean, which is often called the ground line.

The territorial waters of a country are known as its territorial sea. The range of the territorial sea of any country is measured from its coastline, towards the open ocean. Commonly it is somewhere around
12 nautical miles
. India has complete and sovereign rights over this region. The contiguous zone extends
24 nautical miles
from the baseline towards the open ocean. In this zone India has the right to collect customs duty and also carry out economic activities.
The exclusive economic zone of any country extends
200 nautical miles
from the baseline towards the open ocean. In this zone, India is allowed to conduct scientific researches.

chapters.title: Physical Divisions · Eastern and Western Coast

runs: The western coastal area is a narrow stretch of a flat land that lies between the Western Ghats and Arabian Sea. The northern part of the western coastal area is called
Konkan Coast (Mumbai and Goa)
the central part is called
Kanara Coast
and the southern part is called
Malabar Coast
The Eastern coastal area has developed as a result of deltas of rivers like
Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna
and
Kaveri
. Hence the Eastern coasts are very fertile. The region of eastern coastal area falling between Mahanadi and Krishna rivers is called
Northern Circars
The
Coromandel coast
extends from Krishna delta in the state of Andhra Pradesh to Cape Comorin (Kanyakumari) in Tamil Nadu.
The important harbors situated on the western coast are - Mumbai (Maharashtra), Janjira (Maharashtra), Udupi (Karnataka), Kochi (Kerala) and New Mangalore (Karnataka) etc.
The important harbours on the eastern coast are Visakhapatnam (Andhra Pradesh), Haldia (West Bengal), Paradip (Odisha), Kamarajar (Tamil Nadu) and V.O. Chidambaranar (Tamil Nadu).
(a) Island groups of the Bay of Bengal
Among the island groups of the Bay of Bengal the Andaman and Nicobar Islands hold an important place. The Andaman group of Islands is separated from the Nicobar group of islands by a
10º (10 degree channel)
. The width of the channel is approx.
and it lies parallel to the 10º North latitude. The Andaman and Nicobar islands are a Union Territory located in between the Bay of Bengal and Andaman Sea. The highest peak of Andaman island group is
Saddle Peak
which is
meters above sea level. It is located in North Andaman Island near Diglipur.
The highest peak of the
Nicobar island group
is
Mount Thullier
(642m), which is located on the Great Nicobar island. The Andaman and Nicobar island group consists of
836 islands
(Islands/Islets/Rocky Outcrops).
Barren Island,
located in the Andaman Sea lies about 135 km, North East of Port Blair (Now- Sri Vijaya Puram). It is the only active volcano in South Asia and first erupted (recorded) in 1787. The
Narcondam Island
is also located in the Andaman Sea, which is a dormant volcano.
The Andaman island group was formed as a result of the extension of the
Arakan Yoma
(a tertiary mountain range). Limestone, sandstone and shale are the most prominent rock features of this island group.
In the Eastern coastal states of Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, lies
Lake Pulicat

. The lake is famous for being the second largest brackish water lagoon in India after Chilika Lake. Sriharikota Island is situated near Lake Pulicat. The Island separates the lake from the Bay of Bengal.
The
Satish Dhawan Space Centre
is located on this island and it is used by India for her satellite launch programme. The
Adam’s Bridge (Ram Setu)
starts as a chain of shoals from the Dhanushkodi, tip of India’s Pamban island and ends at Sri Lanka’s Mannar Island.

chapters.title: Physical Divisions · Island groups of the Arabian Sea

Laccadive
, Minicoy and
Amindivi Islands

. The Lakshadweep Island lie about 220 km. to 440 km. off the coast of Kerala, with Kochi being the nearest major coastal city. Lakshadweep is a Union Territory with a total area of 32 persons/sq. km.
There are
islands in the Lakshadweep Island group.
The northernmost inhabited island of Lakshadweep is called
Chetlat
whereas the southern end is called
Minicoy
. Minicoy island is separated from the rest of the islands by
9° channels
Minicoy is the
2nd largest island
(4.80 person/sq. km) of Lakshadweep.
Kavaratti
is the capital of Lakshadweep, located on the Kavaratti Island. The largest island of Lakshadweep is
Andrott
or
Androth
(4.90 km²). The Elephanta island is located near Mumbai about 10 km from the Gateway of India.
Salsette island
is in the state of Maharashtra on India’s west coast. The metropolis of Mumbai and the city of Thane lie on it.
Offshore Island - from the deltaic regions of the Ganga to the Eastern and Western coasts of India, to Gulf of Mannar, many islands are located. Among these are

Baida
Nora
Pirotan

Cross

Pigeon
Saint Mary

(near Karwar Coast),
Vypeen
(near Kochi) Shortt Island, Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam Island (earlier Wheeler Island) near Dharma, Bhadrak on the Odisha coast,
New Moore
Ganga Sagar
(in Ganga Deltaic region) are some prominent ones.
Niveshika
is a tidal creeks.

is a
96 km

long tidal estuary in the Rann of Kutch region. It lies on the border of India and Pakistan and has been a disputed area between the two nations. It separates Gujarat from the Sindh province of Pakistan. The dispute lies in the interpretation of the maritime boundary line between India and Pakistan. At present the area is under the possession of India.
Presently India comprises of
28 states
and
8 union territories
. New Delhi is the capital of India. Presently, besides, National Capital Region (NCR) includes Delhi (Whole N.C.T.) and the sub-regions of
Faridabad
Gurugram
Nuh
Rohtak
Sonipat

Jind, Charkhi Dadri

districts of Haryana sub-region;

and

of Uttar Pradesh and,
Alwar
and

According to Office of the Registrar General of India, Ministry of Home Affairs in terms of Geographical area five largest states in descending order of area are
Rajasthan
Madhya Pradesh
Maharashtra
Uttar Pradesh
Gujarat
(196,244 sq. km). According to Census, 2011 in terms of population, the four largest states in India are

Uttar Pradesh shares its boundary with eight states, one Union Territory - National Capital Territory of Delhi and Nepal. The eight states are Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Haryana, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Bihar.
Currently Madhya Pradesh shares border with five states i.e. Gujarat, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Maharashtra.
Bhopal
is the capital of Madhya Pradesh.
According to the Andhra Pradesh Re-organisation Act, 2014, Andhra Pradesh shares a boundary with
Odisha
Chhattisgarh, Telangana, Karnataka
and
Tamil Nadu
Telangana
shares borders with

Karnataka
and A
ndhra Pradesh
. If the

region of Puducherry is also taken into consideration, the number of states/union territories bordering Andhra Pradesh will be considered as six.
Karnataka shares its boundary with six states -

and

Kerala shares its border with two states -
Karnataka
and

. If
the Mahe region

Karnataka

including Puducherry the number of states / union territories will be four.
Punjab shares its boundary with

, Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir and Union Territory of Chandigarh; and it is bounded on the west by Pakistan.

shares its boundary border with

and

The seven sister states in Northeast India consist of Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Meghalaya, Manipur, Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura. Assam shares inter-state boundaries with seven Indian state- West Bengal, Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram, Tripura and Meghalaya and also has international boundaries with Bangladesh and Bhutan. Manipur state covers a 22,327 square kilometer area which is 0.7% of the total land area of India. The hill districts occupy about 90 percent (20089 sq. km.) of the total area of the state, while the valleys occupy only about one-tenth (2238 sq. km.) of the total area of the state.
Phumdi
are a series of floating islands exclusive to the
Loktak Lake

in Manipur state, in north-eastern India. They are made up of heterogeneous masses of vegetation, soil and organic matter in different stages of decay. According to ISFR, 2023 approximately 78.67% of the land area of Arunachal Pradesh is covered under forestry.

Desert of Rajasthan is the most densely populated desert in the world, with a population density of 83 person/sq.km. It is about 10,000 years old. Here only 40% to 60% of the area is suitable for farming. Due to development of the irrigation facilities, there has been an increase in the net sown area which has adversely affected the extension of pasture area.
Karnataka is known as the
‘Silicon State’
of India as it is a hub of information and technology companies. The Silicon Valley of India is a nickname of Indian city Bengaluru which is the capital of Karnataka.
Malnad
(Malenadu) is a mountainous region of Karnataka that is covered with dense forests.
Patland region
is found in the Chota Nagpur plateau area. This area has High hilly peaks, and the maximum part of Chota Nagpur plateau lies in the state of Jharkhand.
The world famous
Kohinoor diamond
was found in the
Kollur mines
of Andhra Pradesh. That is why this state is called as the Kohinoor of India.
Vidarbha

is the eastern region of the state of Maharashtra. Presently, there are two divisions in this region - Nagpur and Amravati. This region includes Nagpur, Amravati, Chandrapur, Akola, Wardha, Buldhana, Yavatmal, Bhandara, Gondia, Washim and Gadchiroli districts of Maharashtra.

chapters.title: States/Union Territories of India · Union Territories

runs: Presently, India comprises of 28 States and 8 Union Territories.
The 8 Union Territories are the National Capital Territory of
Delhi, Chandigarh, Lakshadweep, Dadra
Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu, Puducherry, Andaman
and
Nicobar Islands, Jammu
Kashmir
and
Ladakh
The Andaman and Nicobar Islands are a group of islands at the juncture of the Bay of Bengal and Andaman Sea. The Union Territory of Andaman and Nicobar Islands is located at
latitude and
longitude.
The area located to the north of
10ºN latitude
is called Andaman island while the area to the south of10ºN latitude is called Nicobar Islands. The area of Andaman and Nicobar Islands is 8249 sq. km.
Ladakh is the largest in area among union territories. The population of Andaman & Nicobar is 380581 (according to census 2011). Four Negrito tribes are found in Andaman Islands namely the
Great Andamanese
Jarawa
Onge
and
Sentinelese
. Port Blair (New name - Sri Vijaya Puram) is the capital of Andaman & Nicobar Islands.
Chandigarh and its neighboring region became a union territory on November 1, 1966. This is the capital of both Haryana and Punjab. The area of Chandigarh is 114 km² and population is 10.55 lakh.
Dadra and Nagar Haveli

is surrounded by the states of Gujarat and Maharashtra. It has two parts. The first one is Dadra and the other one is Nagar Haveli. The area of Dadra and Nagar Haveli is 491sq.km and the population is 3.44 lakh (Census: 2011).
Daman and Diu
was a Union Territory of India. It has been divided into two parts Daman (on the Arabian Sea, along the coastal border of Maharashtra and Gujarat) and Diu (on the Saurashtra coast).
Daman
is the capital of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu.
New Delhi
, the capital of India, and the National Capital Territory of Delhi, is a union territory. The area of the NCT of Delhi is 1483 sq. km and the population is 1.68 cr. (Census 2011).
The NCT of Delhi, is the
largest union territory in terms of population
. Lakshadweep is the smallest union territory in India in terms of area (32 sq.km). Apart from this,
the population of Lakshadweep is also the lowest (64473 persons) (Census 2011)
. There are 36 islands in the Lakshadweep. Kavaratti is the capital of Lakshadweep.
Puducherry is divided into four separate districts, two of which (Karaikal and Puducherry) are situated near Tamil Nadu.
Yanam
is located near Andhra Pradesh and
Mahe
is located near Kerala.
The area of Puducherry is 490 km² and the population is
12.48 lakh (Census 2011). Puducherry is the capital of this union territory.
The Constitution of India has not defined the term Schedule Tribes. According to
Article 366 (25)

of the Constitution Scheduled Tribes means to tribes or tribal communities or parts of such tribes or tribal communities as are deemed under Article 342 to be Scheduled Tribes for the purposes of this Constitution. In India tribes are classified as per their cultural specialties, place of residence etc.
Tribal areas of India can be divided into 7 parts - (1) Northern Region,
(2) North Eastern Region, (3) Eastern Region, (4) Central Region, (5) Western Region, (6) Southern Region, (7) Island groups.
The Scheduled Tribes of India constitute about 8.6% of the total population of the country. The largest population of Scheduled Tribes is found in the states of
Madhya Pradesh
Maharashtra
and
Odisha
As per the census of 2011, Punjab, Haryana, Chandigarh, the NCT of Delhi & Puducherry are the states and union territories where no notified scheduled Tribe is found.
As per the census of2011 the largest tribal group of India is
Bhil
, with a population count of17071049.
Gond
is the second largest tribal group of India (pop. - 13256928). Santhals (6,570,807) and Naikda (3787639) are in 3rd & 4th place respectively.
Some of the important tribes of India are as follows
Tharu
- This tribe resides mainly in the
Nainital district

of Uttarakhand, particularly in the Khatima and Sitarganj Tehsils of Udham Singh Nagar district and the Terai regions of U.P. and Bihar. They believe in Hinduism. One unique feature of this tribe is that they celebrate Diwali as a sorrow. They live in joint families and are believed to be descendants of the Kirate clan. It is the largest tribal group in the state of Uttarakhand.
Bhotia

- This tribe resides in the hilly regions of Uttarakhand and the Terai regions of Uttar Pradesh among others. Bhotias belong to the Mongoloid race. The tribe is known for its migratory pastoralist nature.
Jaunsari
- They reside in the state of Uttarakhand and Uttar Pradesh. They practice agriculture and
polyandry
Buksa

- They reside in the Nainital, Dehradun and Pauri Garhwal districts of Uttarakhand and in some places in Uttar Pradesh. The Anulom and Pratilom styles of marriage are very prevalent in this tribe. The Buksa tribe claims to be related to the
Rajput clan
Raji
- This tribe resides in Uttarakhand and Uttar Pradesh and practices Hinduism. Jhum cultivation is very prevalent in the tribe.
Kharwar

- They reside in Deoria, Ballia, Ghazipur, Varanasi and Sonbhadra districts of Uttar Pradesh. They are known for their ill temper and strong physical features. The tribe is the second largest tribe of Uttar Pradesh.
Gaddi

- The tribe mainly resides in Kangra and Chamba districts of Himachal Pradesh and is also found in Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir. The area falls in the Dhauladhar range of Western Himalayas. It is an ancient tribe of the Dhauladhar range having a population of over 1.5 lakh. They believe themselves to be
descendants of Garhwa rulers of Rajasthan
. Other prominent tribes of the Dhauladhar range are Gujjar, Bakarwal, Lahauli, Bari etc.
Gond

- They are native to Gondwanaland hence they got the name Gond. The tribe is found in the states of Bihar, West Bengal, Jharkhand, Maharashtra, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Odisha, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Gujarat etc. For food resources, the tribe mostly depends on hunting and fishing though some shifting cultivation is also practiced. They were few clothes in their attire; however, women are very fond ofwearing ornaments. Animal sacrifice is practiced. The Gond is the
largest tribal group
in U.P.
Bhil

- The name Bhil is believed to have been derived from Villu or Billu, which in most Dravidian languages is the word for “Bow” in reference to the weapon that, until the desert times, they seemed almost always to be carrying.
They belong to the
proto-Australoid
race, and are famous for their Ghoomar dance. They are found in the states of Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tripura, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Rajasthan etc.
Santhal

- The tribe is a native of Santhal Pargana hence they are called Santhals. As per the census of 2011, they reside in the states of Bihar, Tripura, West Bengal, Jharkhand, and Odisha etc. Their physical structure is very similar to that of the
Dravidians
. Rice is their staple diet.
Munda

- The tribe resides in the states of Jharkhand, West Bengal, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Tripura, Odisha etc. The Munda tribe practices many festivals. Mage, Phagu, Karam, Sarhul and Sohrai are some of the important festivals. The festival of
Sarhul
is celebrated every year in the first month of the Hindu calendar, on the third day of the moon or the fortnight of'Chaitra' and is celebrated untill the month of June or 'Jeth.'
Korwa
- Mainly found in the states of Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh and West Bengal. Mostly hunting and gathering is practiced though some of them practice agriculture too.
Kol
- Found in the states of Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra etc. the Kol tribe is mostly agrarian in nature.
Manganiyar
- They reside in the desert regions of Rajasthan and practice Islam as their religion. They are known for their musical/folk legacy. They are also found in the Sindh Province of Pakistan.
Khasi
- Found in the North-Eastern states of Meghalaya, Assam and Mizoram, the tribe practices Jhum cultivation.
Toda
- They reside on the
Nilgiri Hills
, and are also known by the names Todi or Tuda. They claim themselves to be
descendants of Aryans
. They mostly practice
pastoralism
Polyandry
is prominent among the Todas.
Jarawa
- It is the most primitive tribe of India. They reside in the
Andaman and Nicobar group of Islands
. Mostly found on the southern and Middle Andaman Islands their area of residence is protected by law in our country, hence human activity is completely prohibited in the region.
Onges
- They reside in the western part of Little Andaman Island (Andaman & Nicobar group of Islands).
Shompen
- The indigenous people of Great Nicobar, part of the Andaman & Nicobar Islands.
Sentinelese
- Andaman & Nicobar Islands
Naga

- The tribe resides in the states of Nagaland, Manipur, Assam, Meghalaya and Mizoram. They practise jhum (shifting) cultivation and are traditionally known for their distinct handwoven textile and shawls.

Oraon, Ho, Bhumij, Kharia, Soura, Birhor, Khond, Kharwar, Asur, Baiga are some other important tribes of Jharkhand. Bhil, Meena, Garasiya, Sahariya, Damor and Pateliya are some other important tribes of Rajasthan.
The most spoken language in the country is
Hindi

. Bangla is at second place. In world rankings Bangla is in seventh place, spoken by almost 284.3 million people (Ethnologue, 2025). The various languages of the country can be grouped into the following -
Bharatiya European language family - Marathi, Sanskrit, Pali, English, Prakrit, Apabhramsa, Hindi, Bangla, Gujarati etc.
Dravidian language family - Telugu, Tamil, Malayalam, Kannada, Gond, Oraon etc.
Austro-Asiatic language family - Khasi, Santhali, Mundari, Bhumij etc. (these languages are mostly spoken by the tribal people of India).

I. Ganga Drainage System
The Himalayan Drainage System comprises the most famous river systems of India i.e.
the Indus
the Ganga
and
the Brahmaputra
. Most of these rivers are
perennial
in character, obtaining water from the glaciers, springs and rains.
These rivers carve out a number of erosional landforms like
gorges
waterfalls
and
steep-sided valleys,
etc.
Ganga
is the longest river (2525 km.) in India. The five confluences, known as the
Panch Prayag
, are all along the
Alaknanda
. They are, in downstream order,
Vishnuprayag
(Dhauliganga joins the Alaknanda),
Nandprayag
(where NandakinijoinsAlaknanda),
Karnaprayag
(where Pindarjoins Alaknanda),
Rudraprayag
(where MandakinijoinsAlaknanda) and
Devprayag
(where Bhagirathi joins Alaknanda).

The mainstream of Ganga begins at the confluence of Bhagirathi and Alaknanda in Devprayag. Ganga enters the plain area at Haridwar, flowing through the north of Rajmahal Hills, it finally enters Bangladesh by flowing through Farakka in West Bengal. In Bangladesh, it is known as the
Padma
. The Padma is joined by
Jamuna
(Brahmaputra). Further down stream, the Padmajoins the
Meghna River
. Here onwards the whole river system is known as the
Meghna River system
which drains into the Bay of Bengal.
The world’s largest delta (
Ganga - Brahmaputra-Meghna Delta
) is formed between the Hugli river and the Meghna river.
The important
left bank tributaries
of the Ganga are the
Ramganga
the Gomati
the Ghaghara
the Ganda
k,
the Kosi
and
the Mahananda
The Yamuna is the right bank and the longest tributary of the Ganga. It has its source in the
Yamunotri Glacier
on the western slopes of the
Banderpunch Peak
. It joins the Ganga at
Prayag (Prayagraj)
The Chambal
the Sindh
the Betwa
and
the Ken
are the right bank tributaries of the Yamuna, while
the Tons, Hanuman Ganga
and
the Sasur Khaderi
are its left bank tributaries.
The Chambal River
originates near
Dr. Ambedkar Nagar (Old Name - Mhow)
in the Malwa Plateau of Madhya Pradesh. It flows through a
gorge

Drainage System

The antecedent rivers are those streams that originate prior to the uplift of the land surface of an upland or mountain but maintain their original course of flow even after the landmass is uplifted, by cutting through the uplifted landmass. The Ganga river is an example of an antecedent river.

i. Monsoon
The word
‘Monsoon’
is derived from the Arabic word
‘Mausim’
which means season.

Traditionally, the term "Monsoon" refers to the seasonal reversal in wind patterns that brings rainfall, producing distinct wet and dry seasons in many tropical and subtropical regions, especially in South and Southeast Asia but not limited to them. India receives near-about
of its total precipitation from the southwest monsoon. The monsoon is active from
June to September,

which is very important for agriculture in India. The southwest monsoon normally arrives of the Kerala coast (the southern tip of the Indian Peninsula) around the first week of June, though the exact date varies from year to year and may be slightly earlier or later.
Origin of Indian Monsoon
Monsoon is a result of
differential rates of heating and cooling of land and sea.

The sun is vertical over the Tropic of Cancer in summer season, and the northern regions of the Indian landmass get heated. This leads to the formation of low pressure conditions over the Indian subcontinent. On the other hand, the Indian Ocean is colder, so high pressure is generated, leading to northward shifting of Inter Tropical Convergence Zone.
The Inter Tropical Convergence Zone
(ITCZ) is a low-pressure belt near the equator where trade winds of the northern and the southern hemispheres converge.
Due to the northward shift of the ITCZ, the trade winds of the southern hemisphere cross the equator between
and
E longitudes and starts blowing from the southwest to the northeast under the influence of the
Coriolis
force. It becomes southwest monsoon.
In winter, the ITCZ moves southward, and so the reversal of winds from northeast to south and southwest takes place. They are called
northeast monsoons.
The sudden onset of the moisture-laden winds associated with violent thunder and lightning is often termed as the
‘burst’
of the monsoon. The monsoon may burst in the first week of June in the coastal area of Kerala.
The monsoon approaches the Indian landmass in two main branches:
(i) The Arabian Sea branch
(ii) The Bay of Bengal branch
The Tibetan Plateau has a very broad impact on the Indian climatic pattern.

Rainfall received from the southwest monsoon winds is seasonal in character, occurring between June and September. Monsoonal rainfall is largely governed by relief or topography. The monsoon rainfall has a declining trend with increasing distance from the sea. The rainless intervals are known as
‘breaks’
in the monsoon.
The Retreat of the Monsoon -
The months of October and November are known for
retreating monsoons.

The weather in the retreating monsoon is dry in north India whereas it is associated with rain in the eastern part of the Peninsula. The widespread rainfall during this season is associated with the movement of cyclonic depressions that develop in situ over the south-east Bay of Bengal and the adjoining Anddman sea and then cross the eastern coast of the Southern Peninsula. These tropical cyclones are very destructive. A bulk of the rainfall on the Coromandel coast is derived from these depressions and cyclones. Such cyclonic storms are less frequent in the Arabian Sea.

El-Nino

is a complex weather system bringing drought, floods and other weather extremes in different parts of the world. It occurs with the sudden appearance of warm currents off the coast of Peru (warm equatorial current replaces cold Peruvian current).
Generally in India rainfall occurs from the month of June to September when south-west monsoon is effective throughout the country. In this period, the low-pressure zone of
North Western India
is very intense and systematic. Due to low air pressure, south-east winds from the
tropic of Capricorn
in the Southern Hemisphere cross the equator and are attracted towards the Indian Peninsula. Passing over the oceans these winds are filled with humidity and split into two branches -
Arabian Sea branch
and
Bay of Bengal branch
When the south-west monsoon winds enter the terrestrial area, it rains with an intense thundering and torrential storms. The arrival of these winds and rainfall is called
‘burst’
of the monsoon.
The speed of these winds is about 30 km/hon average and they become effective throughout the country within a month.
According to the data Rainfall Statistics of India (2024), almost the entire rainfall is received from the southwest monsoon (June-September).

Monsoon winds of the Arabian Sea are obstructed by the Western Ghats. These winds climb the slope of the Western Ghats and soon become cool causing heavy rainfall on the windward side of Western Ghats. These winds cause little rainfall to the east of the Western Ghats. The region of low rainfall is known as the
rain-shadow area
R

Another branch of monsoon winds from the Arabian Sea causes rainfall in the extensive areas of central India. Thereafter, they enter the Ganga plains and mingle with the Bay of Bengal branch. The Bay of Bengal branch of monsoon winds causes rainfall in northeast and Gangetic plains reaching as far as the Punjab plains.
The actual annual rainfall in India is about
but it has great spatial variations. The highest amount of rainfall occurs along the west coast of the Western Ghats as well as in the Eastern-Himalayan region and Meghalaya.
Mawsynram

receives the highest average annual rainfall in the world. According to the data Rainfall Statistics of India 2024, annually, the District of East Khasi Hills in Meghalaya received the highest rainfall of 6171.0mm whereas the District of Leh in Ladakh (UT) received the lowest rainfall of 56.967mm, which resembles with the normal pattern of rainfall in India.
Mango showers
are pre-monsoon showers in Kerala and Karnataka. They are known as such because they help in the early ripening of the mangoes.

The winter (northeasterly) winds are generally dry over most of India, but after crossing the Bay of Bengal they pick up moisture and cause rainfall over the south-eastern coast of India during the northeast (retreating) monsoon season. Most parts of India
do not
receive much rainfall in the winter season. Some weak temperate cyclones from the Mediterranean Sea cause rainfall in
Punjab
Haryana
Delhi
and Western
Uttar Pradesh
. Although the amount is meager, it is highly beneficial for
Rabi crops
. Central India, northern parts of the Southern Peninsula, Arunachal Pradesh and Assam also receive winter rainfall.

During October to December, the northeast (retreating) monsoon winds, after crossing the Bay of Bengal, pick up moisture and cause heavy to torrential rainfall over the Tamil Nadu coast (Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal), Southern Andhra Pradesh (Costal andhra Pradesh, Yanam and Rayalaseema), South- interior Karnataka and parts of southern Kerala (including Mahe).
Natural disasters are catastrophic events of atmospheric, geological and hydrological origin that can cause fatalities, property damage and socio-environmental disruption.
Volcanic eruptions, Earthquakes, Oceanic Vibrations, Droughts, Floods, Cyclones, Soil erosion, Snow avalanches, Mud Flows, etc. are example of Natural Disasters. Among these
most of the disasters are produced by Natural forces.
However, unwanted activities of human’s increase the intensity of these disasters. Due to the exploitative activities of human beings, the adverse effects of these disasters have increased.

The Himalayan Mountain is a new fold mountain whose growth is still continuing. The collision of the Indian Plate along the boundary of Nepal formed the orogenic belt that created the Himalayan Mountains.
The Indian Plate is moving faster than the Eurasian Plate
in a northward direction. Hence, the associated compression due to this phenomenon has kept the Himalayas growing in size.
The Southern Plateau is relatively more stable, yet the rare events of low intensity earthquakes in the region raise questions about the stability of Peninsular India.

On the basis of data provided by the India Meteorological Department and other agencies, the Bureau of Indian Standards has published the latest version of seismic zone map of India. The Bureau of Indian standards has prepared
‘Earthquake Resistant Design Code of India, IS - 1893, Part I: 2002
which is a new edition of seismic zone mapping of India. In this, India has been divided into four seismic zones on the basis of earthquake intensity - namely
Zone II, Zone III, Zone IV
and
Zone V
. Each zone indicates the effects of an earthquake at a particular place based on the observations of the affected area and can also be described using a
descriptive scale like the Modified Mercalli Intensity
Scale or the
Medvedev-Sponhever-Karnik Scale (MSK).
Risk Zone
Zone III (Moderate Intensity) MSK VII, Moderate Damage Risk Zone
Zone IV (High Intensity) MSK VIII, High Damage Risk Zone
Zone V (Very High Intensity) MSK IX or greater, Very High Damage Risk Zone
Zone V:
Zone V covers
10.9% of the area of the country
with the highest risk zone that suffers earthquakes of intensity MSK IX or greater. The IS code assigns a zone factor of
0.36 for Zone V

. It is referred to as the very high damage risk zone. The region of J&K (UT), Ladakh (UT) some parts of Uttarakhand and Bihar, the North - East Indian region and the Rann of Kutch, Andaman & Nicobar etc., fall in this zone.
Zone IV
- The IS code assigns a zone factor of
0.24 for Zone IV
. The Indo - Gangetic basin and the
National Capital Territory of Delhi
, as well as the rest of Himalayas, are included. in Zone IV. In Maharashtra, the Patan area (Koyananagar) falls under Zone IV.
This zone covers the northern parts of Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal, parts of Gujarat and small portions of Maharashtra near the west coast and Rajasthan. It covers almost
17.3% of the areas of the country
Zone III
- The IS code assigns a zone factor of
0.16 for Zone III
. It covers the the Lakshadweep Islands. This zone is classified as a moderate damage risk zone.
It covers 30.4% of the areas of the country.
Zone II
- The IS code assigns zone factor of 0.10 for Zone II. Zone II is determined by combining the previous Zone I and Zone II. It
covers 41.4% of India.
Major parts of the peninsular region and Karnataka Plateau fall in this zone. Thus, it does not come under the zone of high seismic intensity.
Tsunami
is a Japanese word, which consists of two words,
‘tsu’

meaning ‘harbours’ and ‘nami’ meaning ‘wave’. According to the High Powered Committee on Disaster Management Report (2001) of India, it originates from events like Earthquakes in the Ocean, Landslides, Volcanic explosions, etc. The
majority of Tsunamis originate from earthquakes
that occur on the ocean floor. Tsunami is also called the
‘Harbour waves’
or ‘
Sea waves’
. The
Indian Tsunami Early Warning System (ITEWS)
is established at Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Science (INCOIS),
Hyderabad

. It started operating in October 2007. On 26th December, 2004, a Tsunami, that originated from the Indian Ocean, hit the Coromandel coast of India. The Coromandel coast is southeastern coast of the Indian subcontinent. The coastlines run from
False Divi Point in north
to Kanyakumari in the south.
The
India Meteorological Department
was constituted in
under the Ministry of Earth Sciences, with its headquarters at
New Delhi

The Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology and the deputy director's office of IMD (India Meteorological Department) are situated in Pune. Kolkata was the first head office of India Meteorological Department. The headquarters of IMD was later shifted to
Shimla in 1905
, then to Pune in 1928, and finally to
Delhi in 1944
Floods are an overflow of water submerging land is usually dry. The second important consequence of uncertainty and irregularity of monsoons is the flooding.
“The Flood Forecast & Warning Organisation”
was set up by
Central Water Commission in 1969
to establish forecasting sites on Inter-State rivers in various flood prone areas of the country.
The
‘National Flood Forecasting and Warning Network’
of Central Water Commission, comprises of 338 flood forecasting sites.
The flood region of Uttar Pradesh is divided into high flood prone and low flood prone regions.
A
cyclone
is a large scale air mass that rotates around a strong centre of low pressure. They are usually characterized by spiraling winds that rotate
anti-clockwise
in the Northern Hemisphere and
clockwise
in the Southern hemisphere. Tropical cyclones are characterized by large pressure gradients.
The centre of the cyclone is mostly a warm, low-pressure, cloudless core known as the eye of the storm. Generally, the isobars are closely placed to each other, showing high-pressure gradients.
Under the influence of gravity, a landslide is an activity involving the sliding of rocks and soil along slopes.
The frequency of
landslides
has been increasing in the Himalayas. Its root causes are increased frequency of earthquakes as well as
man-made activities
such as the construction of roads and dams. L
arge scale mining
has been conducted for the construction of roads, dams, and minerals in the Himalayas in recent years. That is why the frequency of landslides has increased in the Himalayas.
The first Disaster Management Training Institute in country
has been established in
Latur, Maharashtra.
The Black soil is also known as the
‘Regur Soil’,
or the
‘Black Cotton Soil’, ‘Tropical Black Earth’
or the
‘Tropical Chernozem’
These soils are formed by the weathering and erosional work of
Basalt Lava
These soils cover most of the Deccan trap especially in the states of Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Telangana. Geographically, it spreads over
5.46 Lakh sq km in different Indian states.
The Black soils are very suitable for cultivation of
cotton
. These soils are rich in
Lime, Iron, Magnesium corbonate, Alumina, Potash and Calcium
. They also contain Potash but they lack in
Phosphorus
Nitrogen
and
Organic Matter
The black
soils are generally clayey
, deep, and impermeable. They swell and become sticky when wet and
shrink
when dried. During the dry season, these soils develop wide cracks. Thus, there occurs a kind of
self ploughing
. Because of this characteristic of slow absorption and loss of moisture, the black soil retains the moisture for a long time.
The colour of Black Cotton soil ranges from
deep black, similer to
the colour of Chestnut.
According to
‘Krebs’,
the Black soil is a mature soil in which special reliefand climate play an important role.
F.Buchanan- Hamilton carried out research on Laterite soil for the first time in 1807. Its name has been derived from the Latin word
‘Later’
which means
‘brick’
These soils are as soft as butter when wet but become harder like bricks when dry.
The laterite soil is formed under conditions of high temperature and
heavy rainfall
with alternate wet and dry periods, which leads to the
leaching
of soil, leaving only oxides of iron and aluminium. The humus content of the soil is removed quickly by bacteria that thrive well in high temperatures.
These soils are poor in
Organic Matter
Nitrogen
Phosphate,
and
Calcium
while
Iron Oxide, Aluminium Oxides
and
Potash
are in excess. Hence, laterites are not suitable for cultivation. However, the application of manures and fertilizers is required to make the soils fertile for cultivation.
They are well
developed in parts of Western Ghats, Eastern Ghats,

South Maharashtra, parts of Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, West Bengal, Kerala, Jharkhand, Meghalaya, and Assam. Laterite soil is widely spread in India and covers an area of 2.48 lakh sq. km. It is
mostly found in Kerala (Malabar Coastal region)
followed by Maharashtra. In laterite soil a common relationship is found between height and chemical composition. The
upper parts are more acidic than the inner ones.
Alluvial soils are widespread in the northern plains and the river valleys. These soils cover about 15 lakh sq. km or about
of the total area of the country.
The alluvial soil is largely found in the Indo-Gangetic plain starting from
Punjab

in the west to the West Bengal and Assam in the east. These soils are also found in deltas of Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Cauvery, where they are called deltaic Alluvium. Alluvial soils are formed mainly by Himalayan sediments and sea retreats.
The colour of Alluvial soil varies from light grey to ash grey. They vary in nature from
Sandy
Loam
to
Clay
Generally they are rich in
Phosphoric Acid, Potash
Lime,
and
Organic Matter
but poor in
Nitrogen
and
Humus content

Due to the cultivation of leguminous crops nitrogen fixation takes place at a faster rate in these soils. They are suitable for irrigation which helps in growing crops like Wheat, Rice, Sugarcane, Jute, Cotton, Maize, Oilseed, Fruits and Vegetables.
Generally loamy soil has 40% sand particles, 18% clay particles and 42% silt particles.
Types of Alluvial Soil:
Khadar
- Khadar is the
new alluvium
and is deposited by floods annually enriching the soil by depositing fine silts. It always remains fertile.
Bangar
- Bangar represents a system of
older alluvium
deposited away from the flood plains. Its color is pale reddish brown and in this, nodules are formed at large scale.
Bhabar
- Bhabar is the
gently sloping coarse alluvial zone
below the Shiwalik Hills, where streams disappear into permeable sediments.
Tarai
- The
marshy lowland region south of the Bhabar
is called Tarai (Terai). The soil of this region is generally rich in nitrogen and organic matter but poor in phosphate. The ancient alluvial soil found at higher altitudes in this region is known as
Rarh Plain
Red Soil
- Red Soil in India, is formed by weathering of ancient crystalline igneous and metamorphic rocks.
The higher concentration of iron is responsible for the red colour of the soil.
These soils are found in regions of low rainfall and are obviously more leached than
Laterite soils.
The red soils cover a large portion of land in India (approximately 3.5 lakh sq. km).
Red soils are
poor in Phosphorus, Nitrogen and Lime content.

They are found in the Indian States of Western Tamil Nadu, Southern Karnataka, Southern Maharashtra, north-eastern Andhra Pradesh and some parts of M.P., Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Telangana and Chotanagpur (Jharkhand). The soil develops a reddish colour due to a wide diffusion of
iron
in crystalline and metamorphic rocks. It appears
yellow when it occurs in a hydrated form
Desert Soil
- The Desert soil covers an area of approx. 1.42 lakh sq. km. The rainfall in these areas ranges from
less than 50 cm.
The
temperature is very high.
The avg. temperature of soil is 35°C. These soils are formed in dry climatic condition. They are
found in Rajasthan, Saurashtra (Gujarat), Kutch, Southern Punjab.
They contain a low amount of organic matter and nitrogen.
Legume crops enrich the soils with nitrogen content by atmospheric nitrogen fixation. Plants contributing to nitrogen fixation include
Soybeans
alfalfa, Lupins, Peanuts
and
Pulses
The soil pH is a measure of the acidity or alkalinity in the soil- pH below 7 is
acidic
and above 7 is alkaline. Generally, the pH value of crop soil is 6.0-7.0.
Acidic soil is
sedimentary
in nature. It has mixed laterite, ferrous red and another red soil group.

These soils are formed by the humid climate, acidic material and geomorphology. Due to temperature, humid climate and heavy rain, rapid erosion occurs in soil and increases the rate of leaching of bases. Due to high temperature with heavy rainfalll, and leaching, acidic soil is formed.
Factors causing acidity in the soil include leaching (due to heavy rainfall), acidic substances, acid-forming fertilizers and soluble salts, etc.
Alkali Soil
Generally, the alkaline soil is found in India in dry and wetland regions. It is fromed due to capillary action ofcations such as
Mg⁺², Na⁺, Ca⁺⁺,
which are deposited on the surface of the soil. This type of soil is mainly distributed in South Punjab, Southern Haryana and West-Rajasthan.
Gypsum (CaSO₄)
is used to change the alkalinity of the soil and remove the salinity from it.
Soil Erosion
- The destruction of the soil cover is described as soil erosion. Soil erosion refers to the
wearing away and removal of the topsoil
by natural physical forces such as water, wind and air.
Topsoil
is the top layer of soil and is the most fertile because it contains the most organic, nutrient-rich substances.
Causes of Soil Erosion-
(1) Deforestation
(2) Disturbance in the natural drainage pattern, improper design of waterways.
(3) Grazing, Water, Wind, Air
(4) Poor vegetation and cultivation
The most affected regions by soil erosion in India are
Badlands of the Chambal and Yamuna rivers,
Western Himalaya (Shivalik region), Chota Nagpur plateau, Malwa plateau, Black Soil region of Maharashtra, arid regions of Haryana, Rajasthan and Gujarat. Ravines of Chambal valley are formed by
Gully erosion
Splash Erosion:
The erosion due to the impact of falling raindrops on soil-surface leading to the destruction of the crumb structure is known as the raindrop or splash erosion. This is the
first stage of erosion
Sheet Erosion:
Sometimes water flows as a sheet over large areas down a slope. In such cases, the topsoil is washed away. This is known as sheet erosion. It is the
second stage of soil erosion
Rill Erosion :-
This is the
third stage of sheet erosion

. If erosion continues unchecked for a sufficient time then rills or small finger-shaped grooves which are a few centimetres in depth may develop on the landscape. Over a period of time, the fine rills increase in number and also become deeper and wider, resembling the twigs, branches and trunk of a tree. This is called rill erosion.
Gully Erosion :-
This is the
fourth stage of erosion.

With further erosion of the soil, the rills may become deeper and enlarge the (region between the Tapti and Sabarmati valleys, and are ultimately turning into gullies. Gully erosion is also responsible for the formation of ravines.
Stream Channel Erosion
:- Water flowing through a channel corrodes its banks and base until a stable base is formed. This form of erosion is known as stream channel erosion.
Soil Conservation
:- Prevention of soil erosion is also called conservation of soil. The soil erosion can be prevented by promoting afforestation,
Crop Rotation, Terrace Farming
, Building Dams, Shelter Belts, Ebankments, etc.
Crop rotation

refers to the practice of growing different types of crops over the same area in different seasons. It enriches soil fertility and helps in pest control. Plants keep soil bound in locks of roots, and thus, prevent soil erosion.
Reduced or zero tillage
of the land in farming is a way of growing crops or pasture year after year without disturbing the soil through tillage. It helps in soil moisture conservation.
Natural Vegetation refers to the flora that grows naturally without human aid and they change their physical stability, shape and size with respect to the environment.
The Type of vegetation found in an area depends on the geographical factors such as
humidity, temperature, soil, rainfall, altitude,
etc. On this basis, there are several types of vegetation found in India.

The tropical evergreen and semi-evergreen forest is usually found in warm and humid areas receiving more than
200 cm
of rainfall and a mean annual temperature above
. The relative humidity of this region is more than 70%.
Due to high humidity and temperature, trees are
very tall
and
intensive
(dense). They are also called as
“Selvas”
There is a different time for leaf fall for different species of trees, due to which the entire forest is evergreen. The tropical evergreen forest in India is found in
Assam, Kerala, West Bengal, The Andaman-Nicobar Islands, Meghalaya, Tripura
, Mizoram and Western coastal plain.
The major species found in the tropical evergreen forest include
Cinchona
Rubber
Coconut
Bamboo
Mahogany
Ebony,
etc.
2. Tropical Deciduous or Monsoon Forests:
Tropical deciduous forests are also called
monsoon forests
. Trees shed their leaves in the dry season to conserve water. The average rainfall in this region is

cm. On the basis of availability of water, these forests can be categorized as Tropical Moist Deciduous Forest and Tropical Dry Deciduous Forest. In India, Tropical Moist Deciduous Forests are found in the eastern slope of the Western Ghats, the northeastern region of the Indian peninsula and the Bhabar and Tarai (Terai) region.
Trees found in these forests include
Sal, Teak, Neem, Shisham and Mango

cm. These forests are found mainly in

and
Mahua

4. Arid Forest:
Arid forests are also referred to as
‘Tropical Thorn Forests’
. They are found in the areas receiving
less than 70 cm rainfall
They include semi-arid areas of
south-west Punjab, South-west Haryana, Rajasthan
and
Gujarat
These forests consist of a variety of grasses and shrubs. In these forests, plants remain leafless for most of the year. Important species found are
babool, ber, wild date palm
khair
neem
khejri
palas,
etc.
5. Delta Forest
Deltaic forest is also known as mangrove, swampy or
littoral forest

. Mangroves grow along the coast in the salt marshes, tidal creeks, mudflats and estuaries. Deltaic forest develops in the deltaic regions of the Ganga, Godavari, Brahmaputra, Krishna rivers, etc. The Sundarban forest is the best example of a deltaic forests.
6. Montane Forests:-

In mountainous areas, the decrease in temperature with increasing altitude leads to a corresponding change in natural vegetation. Mountain forests can be classified into two types: the northern mountain forest and the southern mountain forest.
The Himalayan range shows a succession of vegetation from tropical to
tundra
Deciduous types of forests are found in the foothills of the Himalayas. It is succeeded by the wet temperat type of forests between an altitude of about
m. Evergreen broad leaftrees such as
oak
and
chest nut
are predominantly found here. At about 2000-3000m altitude on the southern slopes of the Himalayas, temperate forests containing coniferous trees like
Pine, Deodar, Silver Fir, Spruce
and
Cedar
are found. These forests are also found in places with high altitudes in southern and north-east India.
Alpine forests grow all along the Himalayas at altitudes ranging between about
meters.
Deodar
, a highly valued endemic species grows mainly in the western part of the Himalayan range at an altitude of about
meter.

The southern mountain forests include the forests found in three distinct areas of the peninsula e.g. the Western Ghats, the Vindhyas and the Nilgiris. Vegetation in these forests is temperate in higher regions and sub tropical in lower regions. The temperate forests are called
sholas
in the Nilgiris, Ana malai and Palani Hills.
Butea monosperma
is called the
"flame of the forest"
. It is also known as Dhak or
Palash
. Palash has been declared as the
state flower of Uttar Pradesh

India is situated in tropical, sub-tropical and temperate climate area. The maximum area of the country comes under a high-temperature zone, except for the western Himalayas, north-eastern-Assam, Meghalaya and some parts of South India.
High evaporation occurs due to high temperatures. Therefore, there is a need for irrigation to fulfill the deficit of moisture in sown crops.

As per Land Use Statistics for 2022- 23, the net irrigated area during 2022-23 was 79312 thousand hectares, out of which 22.85% was accounted by canal source of irrigation, 2.82% by tanks, 49.34% by Tube wells, 13.46% by other well and remaining 11.53% is irrigated by other source of irrigation. The gross irrigated area in 2022-23 was estimated at 122294 thousand hectares, which was 55.75% of the gross cropped area. Indian irrigation projects can be classified into three groups.
Minor irrigation projects
Up to 2000 hectares of
are irrigated under these projects. These include wells, tubewells, ponds, pumpsets, drip irrigation, sprinklers etc. Minor irrigation projects fulfill about
of the demand for irrigation in India.
(ii)
Medium irrigation projects
More than 2000 to 10000 hectares of
area are irrigated under these projects.
(iii)
Major irrigation projects - More than 10,000 hectares of area are irrigated under these projects. 38% of the need for irrigation in the country is fulfilled by the major irrigation projects.

km.

The foundation stone of the
Indira Gandhi canal
project was laid by the then Home Minister Govind Ballabh Pant in March, 1958. It originates from
Harike Barrage
situated at the confluence of the Sutlej and Beas rivers in Punjab. It is one of the world’s largest canal projects, with a total length of 649 km.
The canal mainly irrigates Sri Ganganagar, Bikaner, Jodhpur and Jaisalmer districts of western Rajasthan.
Under the
Gandak project
a 739 meter long barrage was built near the Triveni Ghat on Gandak River.
The construction of
Farakka Barrage

Ten irrigation projects have been completed on the Bharatpujha river and its tributaries in the Palakkad district of Kerala. The
Mangalam irrigation project
is one of them.

Canal system
was proposed by
Captain Dinshaw J. Dasthur

. Later, the name of
K.L. Rao
was added to it. The then Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee inaugurated the development plan

On July 1, 2015, the
Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sichayi Yojana

(PMKSY) was approved to reduce the dependence of agriculture on monsoon and provide irrigation facilities to every farm. The Rural Development Ministry of the Government of India introduced three watershed development programmes untill April 1, 2008. These programmes are the
Integrated Wastelands Development Programme
, The
Drought Prone Areas Programme and the Desert Development Programme
. These programmes were brought under a comprehensive programme known as
Integrated Watershed Management Programme
The main source of irrigation in Peninsular India is
Pond

. Since ancient times, ponds have been used for irrigation in these areas. The land of the Peninsular region is rocky; therefore, it is not possible to construct canals and wells easily. Besides, most of the rivers of Peninsular India are seasonal, which leads to a lack of water availability for canals. In this case, ponds serve as the main means of irrigation. According to data National Compilation on Dynamic Ground Water Resources of India, 2024. Uttar Pradesh (41.15 billion cubic m.), Punjab (26.24 billion cubic m.), Madhya Pradesh (17.90 billion cubic m.) and Maharashtra (15.07 billion cubic m.) are major states of India in terms of current annual groundwater extraction available for irrigation.

i- Narmada Valley Project

The Narmada is the fifth largest river in India. In 1946, a comprehensive program was drafted for irrigation, production of electricity and flood management in the Narmada Basin. In this project, 30 Major dams, 135 medium dams and 3000 minor dams on the Narmada and its tributaries were declared to be constructed.
The Sardar Sarovar Project
has been established on the Narmada river in Gujarat (163 Meters high near Navagam). It has an installed hydroelectric capacity of 1450 MW.

There are two power houses for the Sardar Sarovar Project (SSP). (i) 1200 MW River Bed Power House and (ii) 250 MW Canal Head Power House. Power benefits are shared among Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat in the ratio of 57:27:16 respectively.
The beneficiary states under the Narmada Water Disputes Tribunal (NWDT) water allocation for the Sardar Sarovar Project are madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Maharashtra and Rajasthan.
Medha Patkar
founded
'Narmada Dharanagrast' Samiti'
in February 1986 with the objective of opposing this project. In 1989, several local organizations merged and named it the
“Narmada Bachao Aandolan”
(N.B.A.). The
Narmada Sagar Project
is also known as
“Indira Sagar Project”
. This dam is situated near Punasa in Khandwa district (M.P.) in Narmada town. The target of irrigation of 1.69 lakh Hectares annually and 1000 MW production of electricity has been set.
There are several projects in the Narmada Valley, such as
Tawa, Barna, Kolar, Sukta
and
Matiyari
projects. The irrigation capacity of about 3,98,300 hectares of land has been attained through these projects.
13.50 MW of electricity is produced from the Tawa project.
Various projects have been started at the tributaries of the river Narmada, such as the
Man project
at the Man river, Jobat
(Shahid Chandra Shekhar Azad Sagar) project
on Hathani river and
Upper Veda project
at the Veda river.

Dr. M.S. Swaminathan is widely regarded as the Father of the Green Revolution in India. Under his leadership (in collaboration with Norman Borlaug), semi dwarf high-yielding wheat varieties developed in Mexico were introduced in India and then tested adapted and multiplied for India condition, lealding to the spread of HYV seeds in India. 19.56% respectively in the national output. Next in order of share in the production were Madhya Pradesh (15.99%), Telangana (6.83%), Maharashtra (6.76%), West Bengal (3.44%) and Uttar Pradesh (1.99%).
The share of coking coal in the total coal (2024-25) produced in India is 6.35% and the rest 93.65% is non coking coal.
Major coal fields of Jharkhand are Jharia, North Karnapura, South Karnapura, Bokaro, Chandrapura, Rajmahal, Giridih, etc.
Jharia coalfield
is situated in Dhanbad district of Jharkhand. Major coking coal deposits are situated here. It is mainly spread across the Chota Nagpur plateau, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and West Bengal.
Total coal production of Chhattisgarh in 2024-25 was 204.953 Million tonnes and total storage (1st April, 2023) is 85.26 Billion tonnes.
Korba coalfield
is situated in the Hasdev river basin in Chhattisgarh.
Korba coalfield is an important coalfield of Chhattisgarh.
Coal reserves of Chhattisgarh are found in
Tatapani Ramkola
Bisrampur
Sonhat
Jhilimili, Chirimiri, Lakhanpur, Panchbahini and Sendurgarh
etc.
Talcher
is a major coalfield of Odisha situated in the valley of the Brahmani River in Angul district. Talcher coalfield is managed by
Mahanadi coalfield Limited
which is a subsidiary of Coal India Limited.
Raniganj is a coalfield of West Bengal. Coalfields of West Bengal are
Barjora, Birbhum
and
Darjeeling
Namchik- Namphuk
and
Miao Bum coalfields
are situated in Arunachal Pradesh.
Coalbed methane
and
shale gas
are unconventional sources of energy. Coalbed methane is 90% more pure methane gas extracted from the coal seam. Shale gas is extracted from fine-grained sedimentary rocks.
Shale gas is not only a mixture of propane and butane but it also contains more than 90% methane, 4% ethene, 1% propane and various other gases. Huge
reserves of shale gas
are found in the
Sindhu-Gangetic region
Assam
Gujarat
Rajasthan
and the
coastal region
. Currently, coal industry in India is facing a lot of challenges. Some of them are
low quality coal
deficiencies in coal washing establishment
, higher imports of coking coal, etc.

chapters.title: Energy Mineral · Petroleum and Natural Gas

runs: Petroleum or mineral oil is the next major energy source in India after coal.
It provides
fuel
for heat and lighting,
lubricants
for machinery and
raw materials
for a number of manufacturing industries.
Petroleum refineries act as a nodal industry for synthetic textiles, fertilizers and numerous chemical industries.
It is found in anticlines and fault traps of tertiary rocks in India.

At first, petroleum was detected near Margherita by Assam Railway and Trading Company in 1860. Next, in 1867, the first oil well was drilled in Makum (Assam). The oldest oil deposits in India are in Digboi (Assam). It is situated in the Brahmaputra Valley.
The four main regions of crude mineral oil are –
(1) Brahmaputra Valley
(2) Gujarat Coast
(3) Western Coast
(4) Eastern Coast
Map not to scale

Brahmaputra Valley (Upper Assam Basin) is India's oldest oil producing region,with the first commercially successful oil discovery at Digboi in 1889 and the main producing belt lies in Upper Assam, largely along/near the Noa Dihing and Dihing (Burhi Dihing) river valleys - mainly in today's Tinsukia and Dibrugarh districts and adjoining parts of the Sivasagar belt. Major oil producing centers are
Nahar Katiya
Digboi
Hugri Jan-Moran
Rudra Sagar
Lakwa
and
Surmaghati
Nuna Mati oil refining plant
is situated in Assam. It comes under the authority of Indian Oil Corporation. It was established in 1962 near Guwahati.
Similarly,
Digboi
and
Numaligarh oil refineries

are situated in Assam. Gujarat is placed at first in crude oil production in India during 2024-25 P (as per Annual Report of Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, 2024-25) and placed at second ifwe include offshore crude oil production.
Ankleshwar
is extendes over about 38.98 km square area of Bharuch district of Gujarat. Here, oil was searched for in 1960 and production started in 1961.
Lunej oil production region
is situated in the upper portions of the Gulf of Khambat in Gujarat.
Kalol field
is situated in Ahmedabad (Gujarat). Its major producing centers include
Nawagram
Dholka
Somasan
Kosamba,
etc.
Koyali oil refinery
(IOCL) is located in Gujarat.

The city of Jamnagar was established by Jam Rawal in 1540 in Gujarat. At that time, it was known as Nawanagar. Here the largest refineries in the world have been established by the Reliance Industries. The western offshore region is an important center of oil production in India. Under it, the
Bombay High Basin
is situated about 160 km from the coast of Mumbai. It wasjointly explored by Russia and India. First oil well was dug up here in 1974.
Aliabet Mineral Oil Field
is included in the western offshore region. This oil field is situated near Aliabet Island in the Cambay Basin, about 45 km away from Bhavnagar.
the eastern offshore region of oil fields in India includes the deltaic regions of the
Godavari
Krishna
and
Cauvery
rivers which are highly associated with mineral oil and natural gas.
Narimanam
and
Kovilkalappal
offshore regions produces crude oil in the Cauvery Basin. Deposits of crude oil have been found in the Rajasthan Desert, Bilaspur Tehsil of Rampur district (U.P.) and Jwalamukhi region of Punjab.
Maugalbhagyam
Shakti
and
Aishwarya
are prominent oil-fields identified in the
Barmer Sanchore basin
near Barmer in Rajasthan.
Oil deposits in the offshore region of India is mainly controlled by the central government.
Most of the crude oil produced in India are from this region only.
Crude Oil Production in India
(Quantity in thousand tonnes)
Bombay High, which lies in the offshore region, is the largest petroleum-producing region.
The first terrible energy crisis occurred in India, in 1973 when oil-exporting countries had increased the oil prices by more than 4 times.
According to the Annual Report 2024-25 (Ministry of Petrolieum and Natural Gas), major production 2024-25 (P) of natural gas in India is carried out from the offshore region of the Bombay High Basin.
Leading natural gas producers are
1. Offshore region (25928 thousand tonnes)
2. Assam (3551 thousand tonnes)
3. Rajasthan (1786 thousand tonnes)
4. Tripura (1227 thousand tonnes)
5. Gujarat (1053 thousand tonnes)

The production of natural gas was 36106 MMSCM in 2024- 25 (P). Offshore areas continued to be the largest producer of natural gas (utilised) with a share of 71.81%, followed by Assam (9.83%), Rajasthan (4.95%), Tripura (3.39%), Gujarat (2.91%), Tamil Nadu (2.81%) and the remaining
4.3% of the total production was contributed together by Andhra Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Jharkhand (CBM), Madhya Pradesh (CBM) and West Bengal (CBM).
Hazira
Vijaipur
Jagdishpur (HVJ)
gas pipeline has been constructed by
Gas Authority of India Limited
(GAIL) to transport gas.
Oil exploration and production in India is undertaken by Oil India Limited and ONGC (Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Limited).
Oil transportation and distribution is supervised by
Gas Authority of India Limited
(GAIL).
The largest deposits of Natural gas are found in the
Bombay High Basin

. Besides this Naharkatiya, Moran Region (Assam), Jagatiya, Godha (Gujarat), Mangamdam, Awadi, Virugambakkam (Tamil Nadu) Namchick and Miyao-Pung (Arunachal Pradesh) etc. also have reserves of oil and natural gas resources.

Reliance Industries Limited searched the abundant stock of natural gas in 2002-2003 in the Cauvery-Godavari-6 Basin in offshore region of Andhra Pradesh. Reliance is the first private company in India that is exploring natural gas at depths about 6000 meters below the ocean surface in the offshore region.
According to Hydrocarbon DG (Directorate General), ONGC has estimated 187.5 TCF gas reserves in 5 basins.
(1) Cambay
(2) Ganga Valley
(3) Assam and Assam Arakan
(4) Krishna-Godavari
(5) Cauvery
Hydrogen Exploration Licensing Policy
(HELP) has been replaced by
New Exploration Licensing Policy
(NELP) since April 1, 2016.

Minerals are generally found in the earth's crust in ore form. Several types of the minerals are found in a different regions of India, but these are unequally distributed.

Earlier, India was first in mica production. Mica was declared a minor mineral on 10 Feb, 2015, but it was classified as a major mineral after Gazette Notification S.O. 924 (E) dated 20 February, 2025. In this notification also included three other minerals (Barytes, Felspar and Quartz), which were shifted from minor to major categories. The minor minerals are Barytes (Major), Bentonite, Calcite, Corundum (Minor) & Sapphire (Major), Diaspore, Dolomite, Dunite & Pyroxenite, Feldespar (Major), Fireclay, Fuller's Earth, Granite, Gypsum (Minor) & Selenite (Major), Kaolin, Ball Clay, Other Clay & Shale, Laterite, Marble, Mica, Ochre, Other Calcareous Materials, Pyrophyllite, Quartz (Major) & Other Silica Minerals [Moulding Sand and Flint Stone (Major)], Slate, Sandstone & Other Dimension Stones, Talc, Soapstone and Steatite.
The only producer of
asbestos
as per the data of the year 2013-14 is
Andhra Pradesh
, whereas its largest reserves/ resources (as on April 1, 2020) are found in
Rajasthan
. No production of asbestos was reported in 2023-24 as well as in the previous year and no reporting mines were noted in 2023-24 as well as in the preceding year.
Metamorphic rock is a result of the transformation of existing rock, in a process called metamorphism.
Metamorphic minerals are formed under high temperature and pressure.
Garnet
is associated with metamorphism.
Five leading states in manganese ore production as per the figures of the year, 2023-24 (P) are
1. Madhya Pradesh 1033424 tonnes
2. Maharashtra 1032992 tonnes
3. Odisha 650856 tonnes
4. Karnataka 355057 tonnes
5. Andhra Pradesh 297537 tonnes
Manganese
is mainly found in
Balaghat
and
Chhindwara
districts of Madhya Pradesh and, Bhandara and Nagpur districts of Maharashtra. Manganese extracted from Odisha is rich in iron content and lacks in phosphorus.
Balaghat
is an important district of Madhya Pradesh in the perspective of mineral resources. The major minerals found here are
kyanite
manganese ore
copper
etc.
Nickel is a lustrous, silvery-white metal. It is the fifth most common element in the Earth's crust. Nickel does not occur in a native state. The
largest resources
(as on April 1, 2020)
of nickel
in India are present in Odisha, but it is not mined. The entire demand for nickel in India is met through imports.
Lead

mainly occurs in metamorphic rock (schist) in a combined form with silver. It is also found in Precambrian and Vindhyan limestone. Lead is resistant with respect to acidic matter and atmospheric corrosion.
According to data from the Indian Minerals Yearbook, 2024,
Rajasthan
is the only producer of lead in India. The
Zawar region
is famous for lead production.
Gypsum
is found in large quantities in Churu-Bikaner-Sri Ganganagar belt. It is used for improving soil fertility. It is also used in the health and construction sectors after value addition.
Rajasthan
is the largest (2021-22) producer of Gypsum.
Jaduguda Mine
in eastern Singhbhum district of Jharkhand is famous for
uranium production
. Other uranium production regions are
Domiasiat
(Meghalaya),
Lambapur
(Andhra Pradesh),
Rohail
(Rajasthan) and
Gogi
(Karnataka). In Uttar Pradesh, uranium is found in
Lalitpur
Monazite
is an important ore of thorium, lanthanum, uranium and cerium. It is found in large quantities in the coastal areas of
Kerala
Large reserves of diamond bearing
kimberlite
tracts have been discovered in Payalikhand and Behradih in Gariaband district of Chhattisgarh.

Kolar

districts are famous for gold production in Karnataka. Gold is also extracted from Hutti Gold Mine (Raichur).
Panna
, located in Madhya Pradesh, is famous for its diamond mines.
Vital energy like coal, crude oil and natural gas are used to produce thermal electrical energy in India. The
National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC)
was established in 1975. As per the Ministry of Power, the installed power capacity in India as of December 31, 2025 was 513729.69 MW. In this, thermal energy has the highest share of

i.e. 246941.62 MW. Coal contributes 219610.00 MW, lignite 6620.00 MW, gas 20122.42 MW and diesel 589.20 MW to thermal power installed capacity. The share of other sectors in the total power generation of India is:
hydropower
50914.66 MW, nuclear power 8780.00 MW, and
non conventional energy (renewable energy)
Government of India is going to start an
Ultra Mega Power Project

based on coal with Power Finance Corporation as its nodal agency. Usage of super critical technique is proposed in this project to cut the carbon emissions. Each of these Ultra Mega Power Projects has a capacity of
or above.
Tata Power is establishing an Ultra Mega Power Project in
Mundra
(Gujarat). According to Ministry of Power, initially, following nine (9) numbers Ultra Mega Power Projects (UMPPs) were proposed to be set up in different states:
(i)	 Sasan UMPP in Madhya Pradesh - Coal pithead,
(ii) Mundra UMPP in Gujarat - Coastal,
(iii)	 Krishnapatnam UMPP in Andhra Pradesh - Coastal,
(iv)	 Tilaiya UMPP in Jharkhand - Coal pithead
(v)	 Akaltara UMPP in Chhattisgarh - Coal pithead,
(vi) Bedabahal UMPP in Odisha - Coal pithead,
(vii) Cheyyur UMPP in Tamil Nadu - Domestic coal based,
(viii) Girye UMPP in Maharashtra - Coastal,
(ix) Tadri UMPP in Karnataka - Coastal.
In addition to nine UMPPs originally identified a request has come from some of the state governments for installation of additional UMPPs in their states. These are given below-
(i)	 Two additional UMPPs in Odisha
(ii) 2nd UMPP in Gujarat
(iii) 2nd UMPP in Jharkhand - Deoghar UMPP
(iv) 2nd UMPP in Tamil Nadu
(v) UMPP in Bihar - Banka UMPP
(vi) UMPP in Uttar Pradesh
(vii) 2nd UMPP in Andhra Pradesh.
Neyveli Thermal Power Corporation
in Tamil Nadu is the first plant of South Asia working on lignite coal. Lignite is a tertiary category of coal.
NTPC Farakka Thermal Power Plant
is situated in Murshidabad district of West Bengal. It gets water from Farakka feeder canal and coal from Rajmahal coalfield.
Ramagundam Super Thermal Power Station
is situated in Telangana. Its total capacity is 2600 MW.
Obra Thermal Power Station
was established in 1967 with the help of Russian engineers in Sonbhadra district of Uttar Pradesh.
Bokaro Thermal Power Plant
is situated in Jharkhand.

Ukai Thermal Power Corporation
