Kothagudem Thermal Power Plants
situated in Telangana.
Uran Gas Turbine Power Station
is a gas based power project situated in Raigad district of Maharashtra. It is operated by Maharashtra State Power Generation Company Limited.
The most promising source of energy to fulfill the future demand for energy in India is nuclear energy. India’s
first Nuclear Power Reactor
was established at Tarapur in 1969. Tarapur Atomic Power Station was constructed initially with a boiling water reactor (BWR) that was based on American technology.
Production of nuclear energy requires
uranium thorium
and
heavy water
Uranium is the most widely used mineral in Atomic Power Station as a fuel.

A total of around 513729.69 MW of energy capacity has been installed in the country as of31 December, 2025 which includes 8780 MW from nuclear energy which is 1.71% of the total installed energy capacity.
Rawatbhata Atomic Power Station
was established in 1973 with the cooperation of Canada in Kota.
Map not to scale
Narora Atomic Power Station
is located in Narora, Bulandshahar District in Uttar Pradesh.
Kakrapar Atomic Power Station
is located in Surat District of Gujarat.
Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant

was established with the cooperation of Russia (the then Soviet Union) in Kudankulam, Tirunelveli District of Tamil Nadu through an agreement. Under this agreement, Russia has been building two nuclear reactors for India since 2002. Under the Intergovernmental Agreement in December 2008, Russia agreed to supply four more nuclear reactors to India. All four reactors are in the implementation phase.
Kaiga Generating Station
is a nuclear power generating station situated at Kaiga, near the river Kali, in Karnataka. It has four units.
The First Reactor of the Kundankulam nuclear power plant, which is located in Kundankulam area (district- Tirunelveli), of Tamil Nadu, is a pressurized water reactor.
Mithivirdi Nuclear Power Station

was established with the cooperation of the U.S.A. The project is a part of the Indo-U.S. nuclear deal signed in 2008. In 2015, the 6000 MW project was approved by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change for the coastal regulatory area. This nuclear power plant is located in the Bhavnagar district of Gujarat.

The Jaitapur Nuclear Power Project in India was originally associated with AREVA of France, but the French reactor business is now represented by EDF. The project is proposed at Jaitapur in Ratnagiri district, Maharashtra.
For the nuclear energy, a heavy water plant is required.
Thal Heavy Water Plant
is located in Maharashtra.
Manuguru Heavy Water Plant
is located in Telangana.

There are seven heavy water plants in the country. These are Vadodara (Gujarat), Hazira (Gujarat), Kota (Rajasthan), Thal (Maharashtra), Manuguru (Telangana), Talcher (Odisha) and Tuticorin (Tamil Nadu).
Nuclear Power Corporation Limited is the joint venture of NTPC and NPCIL.
NPCIL has a
stake in Nuclear Power Corporation Limited and
of NTPC. It was established in January 2011.

Hydroelectricity in India is one of the major sources of energy. Hydroelectricity is generated by fast flowing water, which is a renewable resource. It is easiest to develop hydroelectricity in mountainous areas. The first small hydro project of 130 kW. commissioned in the hills of Darjeeling in 1897 marked the development of hydropower in India. The Shivasamudram project of 4500 kW was the next to come up in the Mandya district of Karnataka in 1902, for the supply of power to the Kolar Gold Mines. Now India has a number of multi-purpose projects like the Bhakra Nangal and Damodar Valley Project etc. producing hydroelectric power. National Hydroelectric Power Corporation (NHPC) Limited is the largest hydropower development organization in India, with capabilities to undertake all the activities from conceptualization to commissioning of hydro projects. NHPC has also diversified in the field of solar and wind energy development etc.

NHPC Ltd. was incorporated in 1975 under the Companies Act, 1956. The company is mandated to plan, promote and organize an integrated and efficient development of power in all its aspects through conventional and non-conventional sources in India and abroad. NHPC is a listed company on the NSE and BSE, successfully concluding its IPO in 2009.

Sources of energy that appear in the form of coal, petroleum, natural gas and nuclear energy are commercial resources. Fossil Fuels such as coal, Petroleum and Natural Gas are conventional sources of energy and are non-renew able resources. In contrast, solars and wind energy, biogas, biomass/energy from agricultural residues, geothermal energy, tidal energy, and small hydropower are non-conventional (renewable) source of energy. Renewable (new) energy resources are those that are naturally replenished or restored by natural/cyclical processes within a reasonably short period of time.
The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy gave approval to the Consolidated Energy Policy on 26 December, 2008.

Solar energy is a huge resource of non-exhaustible form of energy. It is used for cooking, water purification, electricity generation, etc. India receives approximately 5 kW per cm² of solar radiation energy for nearly 300 days in a year.

Rampura village (Jhansi district) is the first village in India that has installed its own Solar Energy Plant and is situated in Uttar Pradesh. The first solar photovoltaic plant of 2MW capacity in India is installed in Paschim Bardhaman district of West Bengal near Asansol. Maharashtra is famous for the
Satara Wind Energy Plant
. The suitable states for the production of wind energy in India are Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Karnataka, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Telangana and Rajasthan, etc.

According to the figures of the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy the assessment indicates a gross power potential of 695.50 GW and 1163.9 GW in the country at 120 meter and 150 meters respectively, above ground level. The installed capacity of grid-interactive wind power in the country as on December 31, 2025 is 54.51 GW.

According to the figures of the Ministry of New and Renew able Energy as of December 31, 2025, Gujarat (14820.94 MW) stands first the wind power installed capacity. followed by Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Maharashtra.
State wise Wind Power Installed
Electrical energy produced due to high and low tides in the sea is known as
tidal energy
. In India there are two major areas for Tidal Energy:

1. Rann of Kutch and GulfofKhambhat (previously known as Gulf of Cambay) i.e. the Gujarat coastal area. The maximum tidal range is 8-11 m, whereas the average tidal range is 6.77 m-5.23 m. There is a tidal range of height 5 m approximately, whereas the average tidal range is 2.97 m.
2. Sundarban delta in West Bengal. India’s first geothermal Electric Plant was installed in
Khammam
in Andhra Pradesh (now Telangana) in 2012. The geothermal energy based
Manikaran Electrical Plant

is situated in Kullu, Himachal Pradesh. It is famous for its hot water sources. Electricity produced from hot water sources is generated in the mountain valleys of Manikaran. Hot water sources are also found in Kasol, Kheer Ganga and Pulga in addition to Manikaran.
i. Iron and Steel Industry
The iron and steel industry is a basic industry. The first attempt to make iron in India started in
in Porto Novo (Tamil Nadu), but this factory late failed. For the first time in India, iron was successfully produced by the Bengal Ironworks in
Kulti
in

. In the year 1907, a new factory was established in India by the Tata Iron and Steel Company at Sakchi (Jamshedpur). Where raw iron was produced in the year 1908 and steel was produced in the year 1912. According to World Steel Association data (World Steel in figures), 2025, it is the world’s 10th largest (in the year, 2024) steel company (Tata in Steel Group, 2024) with an annual production capacity of 31.02 million tonnes. Map not to scale
Visvesvaraya Iron and Steel Ltd. (VISL)
was established in the year 1923 on the bank of the Bhadravati River in Shivamogga District of Karnataka. Iron Ore is supplied from the
Bababudan Hills,
while limestone is sourced from Bhandigunda. Due to the lack of local supply of coal supply, charcoal or wood was used for power which was sourced from the
Malnad
forest area. Since 1989, it has acted as a subsidiary of the Steel Authority of India Ltd. It was completely merged with SAIL in the year 1998.
After the independence, during the second five-year plan of India, special emphasis was given to heavy and basic industries under which
Rourkela
(Odisha),
Bhilai
(Chhattisgarh), and
Durgapur
(West Bengal) steel plants were established.
Rourkela Steel Plant (RSP)

, originally set up under Hindustan Steel Limited (HSL) and now a unit of SAIL is located at Rourkela in Sundargarh district of Odisha. This factory was established in collaboration with Germany’s companies Krupp and Demag. It is situated near deposits of manganese and limestone. Iron ore is brought from Odisha's Keonjhar district. Coking Coal is sourced mainly from the Jharia and Bokaro Coalfield (including the Kargali/CCL washery area in Bokaro, Jharkhand), while Talcher coalfield (Odisha) is largely known for non-coking thermal Coal.
Limestone and dolomite are obtained from Birmitrapur. It gets cheap hydroelectricity from Hirakud easily.
The Bhilai steel plant
was established with the help of the former Soviet Union in Bhilai of Durg District in the state of Chhattisgarh on the Kolkata-Mumbai railroad. The
Dalli Rajhara iron ore deposit
supplies iron ore to the Bhilai steel plant.
Hindustan Steel Limited (HSL)-Durgapur

- the Durgapur steel plant was established with the collaboration of Britain near Asansol in the Paschim Bardhaman district of West Bengal. This plant obtains iron ore from the Bolani mines of the Gua area, Coal from the mines of Barakar and Jharia, manganese from Jamda (Keonjhar District) and electricity and water from the Damodar River.
Bokaro Steel Limited (BSL)
Bokaro
-This plant was established with the collaboration of the then Soviet Union at the confluence of the Bokaro and Damodar rivers in the Bokaro district of the state of Jharkhand.

Major minerals required for the iron and steel industry are iron ore, coking coal, manganese, rock phosphate, dolomite and chromium etc. Due to a lack of coking coal in the country, it is imported from Australia.
Generally chromium and nickel are used in the making of stainless steel. Both of these are mixed with iron metal along with some quantity of carbon for the manufacturing of stainless-steel.
The Visakhapatnam steel plant is India’s first steel plant located on a coastline steel plant. Iron ore is supplied to this plant from Bailadila (Chhattisgarh).
The aluminium industry in India was registered in the year 1937 and started producing alumina in 1942, with the establishment of ‘Aluminium Corporation of India’ in J.K. Nagar (West Bengal).
In India, two new aluminium plants Hirakud
(INDAL)
and Renukoot
(Hindalco),
the were set up during the second five-year plan. HINDALCO is a company of
Aditya Birla Group
. It was established in the year 1958 producing copper and aluminium.
In the year 1962, the aluminium production plant of this company was established in Renukoot (Sonbhadra) in eastern Uttar Pradesh. Novelis Inc. was acquired by HINDALCO in May 2007.
Bharat Aluminium Company Limited (BALCO)

was incorporated in Korba in the year 1965. Bauxite is supplied to this plant from Amarkantak (Shahdol, Madhya Pradesh) and Gandhamardan (Odisha) and electricity is supplied from the Korba thermal powerhouse.
BALCO is the first Public Sector Undertaking (PSU) in producing aluminium.

Hirakund

It is now an 'A' Navratna CPSE. It is one of Asia’s largest integrated aluminium institutes.
Hindustan Copper Limited
is located in Khetri, Rajasthan, which is the only company that originally produces copper in the country.
Cement industry mainly depends on limestone. Due to this, the cement industry is mainly located in the areas having an abundance of limestone.

According to the Indian Minerals Yearbook 2022 India stands second in cement production at the global level, after China. The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Ministry of Commerce & Industry, government of India, publishes data on production and capacity of cement in its Annual Reports. As per The Annual Report 2024-25, the total installed capacity of cement plants has been placed at 640 million tonnes. During 2023-24, the production of cement was 426.29 million tonnes which showed an increase of 8.91% as compared to the year 2022-23, which reported a production of 391.40 million tonnes.
Map not to scale

is renowned for its cement industry. Apart from it, cement factories like
Dadri

Churk

Dalla

Uttar Pradesh is also famous for the
glass industry

Firozabad
, in the state of Uttar Pradesh is also known as the
'City of Bangles'
Dalmianagar
is one of the oldest and biggest industrial towns in India.
It is situated on the bank of the Son River in Rohtas district of Bihar.
It is famous for its cement industry.
It was founded by Ram Krishna Dalmiya of the Dalmiya Group of Industries.
The first Indian
cotton cloth mill
was established in

at Fort Gloster near Kolkata, although this mill was a failure. The second cotton mill in India was established by KGN Daber in 1854 (in Mumbai) and was named the Bombay Spinning and Weaving Company. It is considered the true foundation of the modern cotton industry in India.

In India, cotton is mainly produced in black soils. Some of the important centers, such as Ahmedabad, Solapur, Nagpur, Coimbatore and Indore are located in the areas of large scale cotton cultivation. Thus, cotton is produced in only a few regions of India. It is equally important to note that cotton is a pure raw material, in the sense that it does not lose its weight in the process of manufacturing and the slight loss in weight is more than compensated by the use ofsizing materials. The cotton textile industry is spread all over India. Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Punjab and Madhya Pradesh etc. are prime centers of cotton textiles.

Tamil Nadu is a leading producer of mill-made cotton yarn in the country. The presence of numerous spinning mills, a skilled labor force, and the availability, of cheap hydroelectricity are the main factors for good production.
Ludhiana
in Punjab is famous for the hosiery industry. It is renowned as the
industrial capital of Punjab
. It is known for ready-made garments, hosiery items, sewing machines and parts and machine tools.

The then Prime Minister Jawahar lal Nehru formally inaugurated the Ammonium Sulphate factory in Sindri (then Bihar now Jharkhand) on 2nd March, 1952. After that, the fertilizer plant was established in

Phulpur

co operative fertilizer factory

Heavy Engineering Corporation Ltd. is one of the leading suppliers of capital equipment in India for steel, mining, railways, power, defense, space research, nuclear and strategic sectors. set-up in the year 1958 in Ranchi, HEC has acquired expertise in its field through its more than half a century of experience.

Hindustan Machine Tools Limited, formerly Indian Tool, is a state-owned manufacturing company incorporated as "Hindustan Machine Tools" as Bengaluru in 1953. It is a Central Public Sector Enterprise of the Government of India, under the Department of Heavy Industry, Ministry of Heavy Industries. The company manufactures tractors and watches under its watch division as well as industrial machines and tools mainly under its Praga division. It has manufacturing unit locations in Bangalore, Pinjore, Kalamassery, Hyderabad and Ajmer.
Hindustan Aluminium Company Ltd (HINDALCO), a metal flagship company of the Aditya Birla Group, is located in Pipari village (Renukoot) in the Sonbhadra district of Uttar Pradesh.

Indian Telephone Industries Limited,

commonly known as ITI Limited, is a state-owned manufacturer of telecommunication equipment in India. It was founded in 1948 and has six manufacturing units in Bengaluru (Karnataka), Naini, Mankapur, Raebareli (Uttar Pradesh), Palakkad (Kerala) and Srinagar (Jammu & Kashmir), which produce a range of switching, transmission, access and subscriber premises equipment. The largest petrochemical factory is located in Jamnagar, the state of Gujarat in India.

DCI helps to ensure the continuous availability of the desired depths in the shipping channels of the Major and Minor Ports, Navy, fishing harbors and other maritime organizations. The horizons of dredging activities are fast expanding worldwide, and its services are increasing in demand and being put to use in the areas of Environmental Protection, Tourism, Flood Control, Irrigation, Power Generation, Port Development, Mining, Laying of Offshore Pipelines and so on.

India's first expedition to Antarctica was in 1981. In 1983, India signed the Antarctic Treaty, and constructed its first research base, Dakshin Gangotri, during the 1983-84 season. Since the Indus Valley civilization in India, there has been an ancient tradition of road construction. The Grand Trunk Road connected all major cities of northern India from Sonargaon (Bangladesh) to Kabul (Afghanistan).

The capacity of National Highways in terms of handling traffic (passenger and goods) needs to keep pace with economic growth. India has the second largest road network in the world covering about 63.45 lakh km. This comprises National Highways, Expressways, State Highways, major District Roads, other District Roads and Village Roads as under
As of March 31, 2025

In India, among the major modes of transport road transport remains the dominant mode both in termm of its contribution to gross value added and freight transported. As per the National Transport Development Policy Committee road transport carries about 90% of the total passenger traffic and about 67% of freight traffic.
The Nagpur Plan (1943) divided the roads of India into four sections.
National Highways are the most important road systems in the country, which are being constructed and maintained by the Public Work Department and the National Highway Authority.

The first railway on the Indian subcontinent ran over a stretch of34km from Bombay (Mumbai) to Thane on 16th April, 1853.

i. General Concept

The first rational perspective regarding the origin of the planets was probably proposed by a French naturalist ‘Comte de Buffon’ in 1749. According to the number of stars participating in the origin of planets, the scientific concepts have been divided into two parts- (1)
Monistic concept
and
Dualistic concept
Under the Monistic concept, Immanuel Kant’s Gaseous Hypothesis and Pierre-Simon Laplace’s Nebular Hypothesis became famous. Under the Dualistic concept, Chamberlin and
Moulton
Planetesimal Hypothesis, James Jeans and Jefferys Tidal Hypothesis, H.N. Russell and Lyttleton Binary Star Hypothesis etc. became noteworthy.
The latest theory regarding the origin of the universe is the
Big Bang Theory
Georges Lemaitre
(1894-1966) was the first to present the idea of an expanding universe. Later in 1967, Robert Wagoner presented the interpretation of this theory. The Big Bang theory explains how
or
billion years ago universe expanded from a very high density and high-temperature state.
After the explosion, the universe expanded in all directions and different galaxies of different shapes were formed. Thus, the universe comprises of an infinite number of galaxies.
It is estimated that there are appx. 100-200 billion galaxies in the universe and every galaxy is estimated to have
around 100 billion stars.
Our galaxy is known as an
Akash Ganga
or
Milky Way
The shape of the Galaxies varies in shape and size. Some are spiral, some are irregular and some are elliptical.
In 2005, the Spitzer Space Telescope gave clear evidences that our galaxy (the Milky Way) is
barred spiral
in shape, hence disapproving the earlier theories.

The universe is a collection of infinite galaxies. Every galaxy has around 100 billion stars. These stars are formed as a result of the presence of hydrogen and helium gases in their unified form (Nebulae). The gravitational force keeps the gases and dust particles in the unified form. Velocity, high temperature and organizational processes are the factors behind the formation of a star.
The formation of the star passes through different phases. In the first phase, a
proto-star
is formed after that the star enters the second phase i.e., the
main sequence Star

. A star of the size of our sun stays in this phase for around 9 or 10 billion years. After this phase, the fuel of the star i.e., hydrogen starts getting used up to an extent that the star enters the third phase i.e., towards its
death

The lifespan of any star depends upon its size. A star of the size of our sun (one solar mass) has a lifespan of around 9 or 10 billion years. The bigger the star is, the shorter is its life span. For example, a star whose surface temperature is more than 30000 Kelvin and which is 100 times the size of our sun has a life span of only a few million years. After the main sequence life of the star ends, it enters in the elderly phase.
In this phase, the outer layer of the star expands greatly, It becomes a
Red Giant
or
Red Supergiant
After the red Giant phase, a star witnesses an explosion in the form of a
Nova
or
Supernova
, thus entering its last stage of life. Depending upon its size it can end up in- a
Black Dwarf
Neutron star
or a
Black Hole
Sun like small stars
– after the Red Giant phase and Nova explosion if the stellar mass is less than 1.44 solar Masses, the star will end up being a White Dwarf first and then into a Black Dwarf.
Medium sized stars
- after the Red Giant Phase and Supernova explosion, if the stellar mass is between 1.44 to 3 solar masses, then a star can convert into a Neutron Star (Pulsar).
Large size stars
– those which have a stellar mass more than 3 times that of our sun. These stars have the possibility to convert into a black hole after a supernova explosion.
In 1931 Indo-American Physicist
Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar
published his work on the Chandrasekhar Limit. The Chandrasekhar limit which is appx.

times the mass of the sun (1.4 solar mass) determines the death state of a star. Any white dwarf with less than 1.4 solar mass will remain a white dwarf forever, while a star that exceeds this mass is destined to end in life in the most violent of explosions: a supernova, creating neutron stars or black holes.

It is to be noted here that the Chandrasekhar limit is determined after the nova or supernova explosion of the star has taken place. Prima facie it is determined by the mass of the residue of the exploded star.

It is not certain that which of the main sequence stars leave a residual mass under or over 1.44 times of solar mass, after explosion. However it is estimated that stars, with 8 times the size of our sun leave a residue equal to 1.44 times of solar mass after the explosion, and stars bigger than the above ones leave a residual mass of more than 1.44 times the solar mass. The stars of the latter case have the probability of creating
black holes

. The high gravitational force of the black hole sucks in any left residue of the exploded star. The gravitational pull is so strong that it does not even spare passing by objects; with the passing of time the black hole gets smaller in size, until it reaches the size of a grain of sand.

Black hole related information was presented by Dr. S. Chandrasekhar on 11th January 1935 at Royal Astronomical Society of London. He presented the original papers regarding the subject. In the year 1983, a combined Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Dr. S. Chandrasekhar and W.A. Fowler. After a supernova explosion, the star becomes dead. Hence, a supernova is the explosion of a dying star.
The
sun
is one of the stars of our Galaxy, the Milky Way. Its distance from the Galactic center is
7.94 kiloparsecs
or 25,896 thousand light years.
With an average speed of 720 thousand km/hour, it takes the sun approximately 22.5 to 25 crore years for one revolution of the Galaxy (Every star in the Galaxy revolves around the Galactic Center).
Hence the duration of the time required for the sun to orbit once around the Galactic center of the Milky Way Galaxy is known as 1
cosmic year
or 1
Galactic year
A
light year
is a unit of length in astronomy and is equivalent to the distance traveled by light in one year in vacuum (appx. speed of light in vacuum
3 × 10⁵ km/sec)
. Light years is the unit used to measure the distance between the stars. The distance traveled in one light year in the different units is as follows -
In metre 9.461 × 10¹⁵
In kilometre 9.461 × 10¹²
Millimetre 9.461 × 10¹⁸
Astronomical unit 63.24 × 10³
Miles 5.878 × 10¹²

The north and south celestial poles appear directly overhead the earth’s North Pole and south pole respectively likewise the celestial equator is placed directly overhead the earth’s equator and always stays perpendicular (90°) to the poles. The family of the ‘Sun’ is known as the solar system. Eight major planets, dwarf planets, satellites and countless minor bodies (asteroids, meteors, and comets) orbit the Sun to form the solar system. The solar system dates back to about 4.6 billion years.
Originally there were 9 planets in the solar system. Their average distance in ascending order from the Sun is as follows –
1. Mercury (57.9 million km)
2. Venus (108.2 million km)
3. Earth (149.6 million km)
4. Mars (228 million km)
5. Jupiter (778.5 million km)
6. Saturn (1432 million km)
